Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Lani, a seventy-one-year-old Samoan-American patrol officer, had been driving her husband, Mateo, home from the community hall when the rain began. She recalls the exact angle of the headlights cutting through the downpour, the sudden screech of tires, and the way the steering wheel jerked from her hands. She remembers taking the coastal route because the highway was backed up, a decision she now examines with relentless clarity. The impact was immediate. Mateo was thrown forward, then back. The glass rained down. She pulled the wheel hard to the right, slamming into the guardrail before the other vehicle, a delivery truck, struck her driver’s side. Beneath the hiss of the radiator and the distant wail of sirens, she caught the heavy scent of alcohol on the other driver’s breath and on the steering wheel of the truck. In the years since, Lani’s mind does not soften the edges of that night. When quiet catches her off guard, she is certain she can still hear the metallic groan of the roof caving in and the wet, ragged gasps Mateo made before the medics arrived. Her memories are locked in high definition: the spiderweb fracture of the windshield, the way the dashboard warning lights blinked amber, the exact shade of red on the asphalt. She cannot look away from these pictures. They do not fade; they simply wait for the right moment to surface. Her work as a veteran patrol officer places her directly in the path of what she dreads. During a late-night shift last month, she turned onto a familiar residential street and watched a silver sedan spin out on a patch of black ice, its fender kissing a mailbox with a dull thud. Lani’s hands tightened on her steering wheel until her knuckles whitened. She drove past the scene faster than protocol suggested, leaving it to dispatch. At the station, when two junior officers began debating the causes of a recent interstate pileup over their morning coffee, the words hung in the air like smoke. Lani stood, muttered an excuse about paperwork, and retreated to the evidence room. Even the scent of stale whiskey drifting from a call log folder at a roadside checkpoint brought her to a halt in the damp November air; her chest tightened until she had to roll down the window and breathe. These appraisals lived alongside her memories. Lani had come to believe the crash happened because of the way she acted. At the same time, she held a quiet conviction that she simply could not stop bad things from happening to her. Alongside these thoughts rested the unshakable sense that she should have protected others and she failed. The triggers emerged during patrol, while the memories surfaced independently of her judgments. Her avoidance habits grew quietly over weeks and months, accumulating consequences that changed her work and her home. Mateo noticed the extra space between them when she refused to ride in his car. Her supervisor noted her reduced visibility during weekend shifts after she declined an invitation to co-chair the senior center’s driving safety workshop, citing shift fatigue. The routines shifted around the edges of what she would no longer do. Now, Lani finds herself standing outside the county behavioral health clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, her badge heavy against her hip. The rain outside mirrors the weather from three years ago, and for a moment she considers turning around, but the familiar exhaustion of carrying the night alone keeps her feet planted. She has come to seek help because the silence in her own home has grown louder than the sirens she used to chase, and because she is finally afraid she will never stop bracing for the next impact. What she hopes for, more than she knows how to say, is to sit in a room and learn how to set the weight down, if only for an hour.
